Helium. A colorless, odorless, tasteless, and chemically inert monatomic gas that sits at the top of the noble gas group. It's the second lightest and second most abundant element in the entire observable universe, produced largely through stellar nucleosynthesis. On Earth, helium is actually quite rare, primarily extracted from natural gas deposits where it accumulates from the radioactive decay of heavy elements.

Pierre Janssen and Norman Lockyer discovered helium spectroscopically during a solar eclipse in 1868 and named it after Helios, the Greek sun god. At extremely low temperatures, helium becomes a superfluid. Below the Lambda point at about two point seventeen Kelvin, it flows with zero viscosity and forms a Rollin film that creeps up the sides of containers. Helium has the lowest boiling point of any element at four point two Kelvin, and the lowest melting point as well. In fact, you cannot solidify helium at standard pressure even at absolute zero. Commercially, helium is extracted from natural gas through fractional distillation, particularly from helium-rich fields like the Cliffside Gas Field in Texas. It's used widely in cryogenics to cool superconducting magnets in MRI machines, and as a non-reactive lifting gas for balloons. Hydrogen is the only element lighter than helium, and the two undergo fusion in stellar cores. Uranium decay in Earth's crust is the primary source of terrestrial helium. Neon is the noble gas directly below helium in the periodic table.
